title: Practice Set 1 — Why Fabric Exists
description: Identify platform sprawl symptoms in NordGrid's pre-Fabric architecture, match data engineering tasks to Fabric workloads, classify SaaS-managed vs engineer-managed responsibilities, assign NordGrid data items to medallion layers, predict capacity consumption patterns, and trace a meter reading's journey through every Fabric component.

metadata.foundationException: Module F1 is entirely conceptual — it teaches why Fabric exists, the SaaS model, workload taxonomy, medallion architecture, and capacity basics. No code is introduced until Module F5. Per §4.3, this practice set uses 3 concept identification + 3 output prediction tasks with zero write-the-code tasks. The final task (output_prediction) serves as the module synthesis, combining 5 concepts across the module. The normal §4.2 max of 2 per task type is exceeded under the §4.3 Foundation exception.

description.context: Platform sprawl is the data-platform anti-pattern where the same data is COPIED into separate systems, where each tool has its OWN security model and billing, and where teams cannot see each other's data. Symptoms: duplicated copies of the same dataset, separate access policies per tool, no single source of truth, no cross-team visibility. A UNIFIED platform stores data once, applies governance once, and lets teams query a shared canonical copy with role-based access. Note: row/column-level security and partitioning are NOT sprawl — they are governance applied to a single shared store. The distinguishing question is always: 'is the underlying storage shared, or copied?'.
description.task: For each situation, identify whether it is a symptom of platform sprawl or a characteristic of a unified platform.
description.validationHint: Platform sprawl means data is duplicated, tools are fragmented, security is inconsistent, or teams cannot see each other's data. A unified platform means shared storage, shared governance, and cross-team visibility.

fields.label: The billing team stores meter readings in their own Azure SQL Database. The operations team stores the same readings in a separate ADLS Gen2 account. Neither team can query the other's copy.
options: Platform sprawl — the same dataset is physically duplicated into two isolated stores with separate access controls and no cross-team query path. Two copies of one truth = fragmentation.
Unified platform — each team owns the optimized storage their workload needs (SQL for billing, ADLS for ops); team-specific stores are a best practice when workloads differ.
Neither — this is standard data partitioning where billing rows live in one store and operations rows live in another, split by team responsibility.
fields.correctAnswer: Platform sprawl — the same dataset is physically duplicated into two isolated stores with separate access controls and no cross-team query path. Two copies of one truth = fragmentation.
fields.rationale: The distinguishing fact is that 'the same readings' exist in two physically separate stores with no shared query path. That is duplication, which is the textbook sprawl symptom. A unified platform would have ONE physical copy in OneLake (or equivalent) with role-based access carving out what each team sees. The most common Junior confusion is treating tool-per-team as 'best practice' — it is only best practice when each tool reads from a SHARED store, not when each tool maintains its own copy.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Reframes duplication as 'optimization' — two copies of the same data is fragmentation regardless of which engine each copy uses.

Option C: Confuses partitioning (one logical store split by key, all teams can query) with duplication (two physical stores, neither team can query the other).

fields.label: All NordGrid teams query the same Delta tables in OneLake. The billing team sees billing-relevant columns, the operations team sees operational columns, but the underlying data is stored once.
options: Platform sprawl — different teams seeing different columns is itself fragmentation; if teams can't see ALL columns the platform is not truly unified.
Unified platform — one physical Delta store, one canonical truth, with column-level governance carving out what each role sees. Stored once, governed once, queried by all.
Platform sprawl — Delta tables should not be shared across teams; each team needs its own table for isolation and performance.
fields.correctAnswer: Unified platform — one physical Delta store, one canonical truth, with column-level governance carving out what each role sees. Stored once, governed once, queried by all.
fields.rationale: Single physical storage + role-based column-level access = unified platform. Different teams seeing different columns is GOVERNANCE applied to one shared store, not duplication. The most common Junior confusion is equating 'different views' with 'different data' — but in a unified platform, views differ while the underlying file is shared.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Confuses access-control views (governance) with physical fragmentation (sprawl). Column-level RBAC is a unified-platform feature.

Option C: Invents a rule that Delta tables shouldn't be shared. Sharing a single Delta store across teams is precisely the unified-platform design.

fields.label: NordGrid's data engineers manage their Spark clusters on Azure HDInsight. The analytics team uses a separate Azure Synapse workspace. The reporting team uses a standalone Power BI tenant. Each tool has its own security model and billing.
options: Unified platform — each workload runs on the best tool for it (Spark for engineers, Synapse for analytics, Power BI for reporting); 'best-of-breed per workload' is the unified design.
Platform sprawl — three tools with three separate security models, three billing surfaces, and no shared storage. Tool diversity is fine; security and storage fragmentation is sprawl.
Neither — this is a standard microservices architecture, where each service owns its own data and security, by design.
fields.correctAnswer: Platform sprawl — three tools with three separate security models, three billing surfaces, and no shared storage. Tool diversity is fine; security and storage fragmentation is sprawl.
fields.rationale: The sprawl symptom here is NOT having three tools — it's that the three tools each maintain their own security model, billing, and storage. A unified Fabric setup also has multiple workloads (Data Engineering, Synapse-style SQL, Power BI), but they share OneLake, share Microsoft Entra identity, and share capacity-based billing. The most common Junior confusion is treating multi-tool == sprawl; in reality multi-tool is fine if storage and security are shared.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Confuses 'best tool per workload' with sprawl. The issue isn't tool choice; it's fragmented security/billing/storage.

Option C: Misapplies microservices to data platforms. Microservices are for stateless app code; data platforms benefit from a shared store, not per-service silos.

fields.label: NordGrid's security team applies sensitivity labels and access policies once in Microsoft Purview. These policies automatically govern data across all Fabric workspaces — notebooks, pipelines, SQL queries, and Power BI reports.
options: Platform sprawl — a single security system controlling everything is a single point of failure; consolidating governance creates risk by removing tool-level isolation.
Unified platform — Purview defines policies once and Fabric enforces them everywhere (notebooks, pipelines, SQL, Power BI). One governance plane, consistent across all workloads.
Platform sprawl — Purview is a separate tool from Fabric, so security still lives outside the platform and counts as fragmentation.
fields.correctAnswer: Unified platform — Purview defines policies once and Fabric enforces them everywhere (notebooks, pipelines, SQL, Power BI). One governance plane, consistent across all workloads.
fields.rationale: Centralized governance applied uniformly across workloads is the unified-platform pattern. Purview is the governance plane that integrates natively with Fabric — sensitivity labels, lineage, and access policies set in Purview flow through to every Fabric artifact. The most common Junior confusion is reading 'separate product' and assuming separate-product = fragmentation; Purview is a peer governance plane that Fabric defers to, not an isolated silo.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Conflates 'single' with 'fragile'. Centralized governance reduces drift; it is not a single point of failure in this sense.

Option C: Misunderstands Purview's integration with Fabric. Purview labels propagate into Fabric via native integration.

tasks.title: Match NordGrid's Tasks to Fabric Workloads

description.context: Microsoft Fabric is one product made of multiple WORKLOADS — each workload is a specialized engine optimized for a specific kind of work, but all share OneLake and capacity. The five core workloads to know at Junior level: (1) Data Engineering runs Spark notebooks for batch transformation in Python/Scala/SQL. (2) Data Factory orchestrates pipelines and Copy activities — moving and scheduling data, not transforming it in-flight. (3) Data Warehouse runs T-SQL on a serverless SQL engine with persistent stored aggregates. (4) Real-Time Intelligence (RTI) handles streaming/event-time data with sub-second latency via eventstreams + KQL. (5) Power BI builds interactive dashboards on top of Gold-layer data via semantic models. The trick is to match the task's verb (transform, copy, query, stream, visualize) to the workload's job.
description.task: For each NordGrid task, select the Fabric workload that handles it.
description.validationHint: Each workload has a distinct purpose: Data Engineering runs Spark notebooks, Data Factory orchestrates pipelines and copies data, Data Warehouse handles T-SQL workloads, Real-Time Intelligence processes streaming data, and Power BI delivers reports and dashboards.

fields.label: Transform 500,000 daily meter readings from raw CSV into validated Delta tables using PySpark code in a notebook.
options: Data Engineering — PySpark notebooks running on Spark are the Data Engineering workload's core job (batch transformation in code).
Data Factory — pipelines orchestrate transformations, including running PySpark transformation logic inside the Copy activity.
Data Warehouse — handles tabular transformation with T-SQL, including PySpark code submitted as SQL stored procedures.
Real-Time Intelligence — daily batch notebooks count as a stream of one batch per day, so RTI is the right workload for any scheduled batch.
fields.correctAnswer: Data Engineering — PySpark notebooks running on Spark are the Data Engineering workload's core job (batch transformation in code).
fields.rationale: Data Engineering is the Fabric workload that owns Spark notebooks (PySpark / Scala / Spark SQL). Batch transformation in code lives here. The most common Junior confusion is mixing up Data Engineering (the engine that RUNS notebooks) with Data Factory (the engine that SCHEDULES and ORCHESTRATES them). Notebook code = Data Engineering; pipeline schedule wrapping the notebook = Data Factory.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Data Factory orchestrates and copies, it does not execute PySpark transformations.

Option C: Data Warehouse runs T-SQL only; it does not run PySpark notebooks.

Option D: RTI is for sub-second streaming via eventstreams/KQL, not daily batches.

fields.label: Copy raw CSV files from NordGrid's external SFTP server into a Lakehouse every morning at 06:00, then trigger the transformation notebook to run.
options: Data Engineering — notebooks can read directly from SFTP and self-schedule via the workspace, so this whole task fits in a single notebook.
Data Factory — pipelines own external ingestion (Copy activity from SFTP), scheduling (06:00 trigger), and orchestrating downstream notebook runs. All three responsibilities live here.
Data Warehouse — T-SQL pipelines can include FILE-COPY commands and schedule notebook activations as SQL Agent jobs.
Power BI — dataflows can ingest CSV from SFTP and chain into notebook activations through Power BI's scheduled refresh service.
fields.correctAnswer: Data Factory — pipelines own external ingestion (Copy activity from SFTP), scheduling (06:00 trigger), and orchestrating downstream notebook runs. All three responsibilities live here.
fields.rationale: Data Factory pipelines are Fabric's orchestration + ingestion workload. Copy activity moves files from external sources (SFTP, S3, HTTP, on-prem databases) into OneLake; pipeline triggers handle the schedule; Notebook activities chain runs. Three jobs, one workload. The most common Junior confusion is thinking 'the notebook runs the pipeline' — it's the other way around: the pipeline runs the notebook.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Notebooks transform; they don't own external ingestion or scheduling.

Option C: Data Warehouse is for T-SQL queries against tables, not file ingestion.

Option D: Power BI dataflows refresh BI datasets; they don't trigger notebooks for downstream pipelines.

fields.label: Compute monthly energy consumption totals per region using T-SQL queries, store pre-computed aggregates, and serve them to analysts who write ad-hoc SQL.
options: Data Engineering — PySpark notebooks can write SQL-style aggregates to Delta and analysts can query them with Spark SQL, which is functionally equivalent.
Data Factory — Copy activity can run a SQL aggregation as it moves data, materializing the result into a staging table that analysts query.
Data Warehouse — full T-SQL engine with persistent stored aggregates and an ad-hoc SQL surface for analysts. This is the workload built for the job.
Real-Time Intelligence — KQL queries compute aggregates faster than T-SQL, and the KQL database can serve them to analysts in real time.
fields.correctAnswer: Data Warehouse — full T-SQL engine with persistent stored aggregates and an ad-hoc SQL surface for analysts. This is the workload built for the job.
fields.rationale: Fabric Data Warehouse is the T-SQL workload designed for persistent aggregate storage and ad-hoc SQL by analysts. It supports CREATE TABLE, INSERT, full DML, and the ANSI T-SQL surface analysts know. The Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint is read-only and not the right home for stored aggregates. The most common Junior confusion is thinking Lakehouse + SQL endpoint = Data Warehouse; they are different artifacts with different write semantics.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark SQL is not T-SQL; analysts who 'write ad-hoc SQL' typically expect T-SQL syntax and the Warehouse engine.

Option B: Data Factory's Copy activity is for movement, not for hosting persistent aggregates.

Option D: RTI is for streaming/event-time data; KQL is its own dialect and not what 'T-SQL' analysts expect.

fields.label: Process SCADA telemetry from 2,000 wind turbines arriving every 10 seconds, detect anomalies within 30 seconds, and alert the operations team.
options: Data Engineering — a Spark structured-streaming notebook can read 10-second SCADA windows and emit anomalies; Data Engineering covers any streaming workload in code.
Data Factory — pipelines triggered every 30 seconds can pull SCADA data and apply anomaly thresholds in the Copy activity's data-flow expressions.
Data Warehouse — store-then-query: the Warehouse holds streaming data and a scheduled T-SQL query every 30 seconds runs the anomaly check.
Real-Time Intelligence — eventstreams ingest 10-second telemetry, KQL processes events with sub-second latency, and Activator/Reflex sends operations-team alerts. Built for this job.
fields.correctAnswer: Real-Time Intelligence — eventstreams ingest 10-second telemetry, KQL processes events with sub-second latency, and Activator/Reflex sends operations-team alerts. Built for this job.
fields.rationale: Real-Time Intelligence is the Fabric workload purpose-built for event-time streaming with sub-second latency. It bundles eventstreams (ingestion), KQL databases (event-time queries), and Activator (Reflex) for action-on-event. The 10-second arrival rate + 30-second SLA combination is RTI's wheelhouse. The most common Junior confusion is using Spark structured streaming inside Data Engineering for everything 'stream-y' — possible, but not the right tool for sub-second SLAs that come with real-time alerting.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark streaming exists but is micro-batch by default and not the right SLA fit for 30-second action alerts.

Option B: Data Factory pipelines have minute-level granularity at best.

Option C: Store-then-query loses the latency budget needed for 30-second alerts.

fields.label: Build an interactive dashboard showing NordGrid's regional energy trends, with filters for region, date range, and customer type, refreshed automatically from Gold-layer tables.
options: Data Engineering — Spark notebooks can render interactive HTML widgets and embed dashboards directly in the workspace for business users.
Data Factory — pipeline activities include a Visualize step that renders dashboard tiles tied to scheduled refreshes.
Data Warehouse — T-SQL dynamic views with parameterized filters (region, date range, customer type) are queried directly by browsers and rendered as a dashboard.
Power BI — semantic model + report on top of Gold tables, with slicers (region/date/customer type) and Direct Lake refresh against OneLake. The Fabric workload for end-user dashboards.
fields.correctAnswer: Power BI — semantic model + report on top of Gold tables, with slicers (region/date/customer type) and Direct Lake refresh against OneLake. The Fabric workload for end-user dashboards.
fields.rationale: Power BI is the Fabric workload that builds dashboards for business users — semantic models (defining measures and relationships) plus reports (visuals, slicers, filters). With Direct Lake mode, Power BI reads Gold data straight from OneLake without import or DirectQuery. The most common Junior confusion is producing the data in one workload (DE/DF/DW) and assuming THAT workload also does the visualization — Fabric's design separates production (where data is shaped) from consumption (Power BI).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Notebook visualization is for engineers, not business users.

Option B: Data Factory has no visualization layer.

Option C: Warehouse views serve data but do not render interactive dashboards.

description.context: Fabric is delivered as SaaS (Software-as-a-Service). The line between platform-managed and engineer-managed responsibilities is sharp: the PLATFORM handles INFRASTRUCTURE (compute provisioning, OS patching, storage durability, replication, scaling); the ENGINEER handles DATA DECISIONS (schema, partition keys, data quality rules, pipeline business logic, role assignments). The rule of thumb: anything that requires knowing 'what the data means at NordGrid' is the engineer's job; anything that is generic infrastructure plumbing is the platform's job. SaaS also means engineers have NO access to the underlying nodes — there is no 'cluster console' to log into.
description.task: For each responsibility, predict whether Fabric's SaaS platform handles it automatically or whether NordGrid's data engineer handles it.
description.validationHint: SaaS handles infrastructure: compute provisioning, patching, storage durability, scaling. Engineers handle data decisions: schema design, data quality logic, pipeline business logic, access policy configuration.

fields.label: Provisioning and starting the Spark cluster when a notebook runs.
options: Fabric handles this automatically — Spark sessions spin up on demand from the capacity pool. Engineers don't size, start, or stop clusters; the platform does.
The data engineer provisions the cluster manually with cluster_create() before running the notebook, the same way HDInsight or Databricks classic works.
The workspace admin must pre-allocate Spark nodes each morning to guarantee capacity for the day's runs.
fields.correctAnswer: Fabric handles this automatically — Spark sessions spin up on demand from the capacity pool. Engineers don't size, start, or stop clusters; the platform does.
fields.rationale: Compute provisioning is generic infrastructure — Fabric's SaaS layer handles it on demand from the capacity pool. There is no 'cluster create' step, no node count to pick. The most common Junior confusion is importing the IaaS mental model from HDInsight or Databricks classic where engineers managed clusters; in Fabric you just open the notebook and start running.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Describes the IaaS model. Fabric's SaaS abstraction removes manual cluster management.

Option C: Invents a pre-allocation step that does not exist in Fabric.

fields.label: Designing the schema for NordGrid's Silver meter readings table (which columns, which types, which partition key).
options: Fabric handles this automatically — it infers the optimal schema from the source data, including type-tightening from string to date and a sensible partition key.
The data engineer designs the schema — choosing columns, types, and partition key requires NordGrid business knowledge that the platform does not have.
The workspace admin defines all schemas through portal settings; engineers only write the transformation code.
fields.correctAnswer: The data engineer designs the schema — choosing columns, types, and partition key requires NordGrid business knowledge that the platform does not have.
fields.rationale: Schema design is a DATA DECISION that requires knowing NordGrid's business rules: which columns matter, what types enforce business invariants (e.g., daily_kw can't be negative), what partition key matches the query pattern. Fabric can infer types during file reads (a convenience) but production schema design — selecting columns, choosing types, picking the partition key — is the engineer's job. The most common Junior confusion is conflating inferSchema=True (a notebook convenience) with production schema authoring; they are different scopes.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Confuses inferSchema convenience with production schema design.

Option C: Invents a portal feature for schema authoring; schemas are defined in code or in DDL by engineers.

fields.label: Patching the operating system and updating security fixes on the nodes that run Spark jobs.
options: The data engineer applies OS patches during a weekly maintenance window via SSH into Fabric Spark nodes.
Fabric handles this automatically — OS patches and security updates are part of the SaaS infrastructure layer; engineers cannot and do not access the underlying nodes.
NordGrid's IT security team patches Fabric nodes through Azure Update Manager as part of corporate compliance.
fields.correctAnswer: Fabric handles this automatically — OS patches and security updates are part of the SaaS infrastructure layer; engineers cannot and do not access the underlying nodes.
fields.rationale: OS patching is pure infrastructure — Fabric's SaaS contract includes it. Engineers and admins have NO node-level access to patch (or break) anything. The most common Junior confusion is bringing IaaS expectations: in HDInsight or self-managed Databricks the engineer (or platform team) patched VMs; in Fabric, those nodes are invisible.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Requires SSH-into-node access that Fabric SaaS does not expose.

Option C: Update Manager covers Azure VMs you own; Fabric's underlying nodes are not user-managed VMs.

fields.label: Writing the PySpark code that filters out invalid meter readings (null meter_id, negative daily_kw) before promoting data from Bronze to Silver.
options: Fabric handles this automatically — built-in data quality rules detect and filter invalid records when promoting from Bronze to Silver layers.
The data engineer writes this logic — Fabric does not know that 'negative daily_kw' is invalid at NordGrid; that's a business rule only the engineer can encode.
The Data Factory pipeline's Copy activity detects and removes invalid records during ingestion based on the schema in the Lakehouse.
fields.correctAnswer: The data engineer writes this logic — Fabric does not know that 'negative daily_kw' is invalid at NordGrid; that's a business rule only the engineer can encode.
fields.rationale: Data quality logic is the engineer's job. 'Negative daily_kw is invalid' is a NordGrid business rule — Fabric has no way to know that; the engineer must write the filter. The platform handles infrastructure (running the notebook, durable storage); business semantics belong to the team. The most common Junior confusion is hoping Fabric has 'auto-clean' built in; data quality is always domain-specific.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Overstates Fabric. There is no built-in 'invalid record' detector that knows business rules.

Option C: Copy activity moves data; it does not enforce business validity rules.

fields.label: Replicating OneLake data across availability zones to protect against hardware failure.
options: The data engineer configures replication mode (LRS/ZRS/GRS) in the Lakehouse settings, just like any ADLS Gen2 account.
Fabric handles this automatically — OneLake inherits ADLS Gen2 replication built into the SaaS contract; engineers don't pick LRS vs ZRS.
NordGrid must purchase a separate disaster-recovery license to enable OneLake cross-zone replication.
fields.correctAnswer: Fabric handles this automatically — OneLake inherits ADLS Gen2 replication built into the SaaS contract; engineers don't pick LRS vs ZRS.
fields.rationale: Storage durability is infrastructure — Fabric's SaaS contract includes it. OneLake sits on ADLS Gen2 with replication baked in; engineers don't choose LRS/ZRS/GRS. The most common Junior confusion is importing the IaaS Azure-storage knob set; in OneLake those knobs are abstracted away.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Fabric does not surface LRS/ZRS settings — that's IaaS thinking.

Option C: Invents a separate DR license. Replication is included.

fields.label: Deciding which NordGrid team members can access the Silver workspace and what actions they can perform.
options: Fabric handles this automatically — by default all users in the tenant can access all workspaces, so no manual configuration is needed.
The data engineer or workspace admin assigns roles (Admin / Member / Contributor / Viewer) — Fabric enforces the roles but does not decide who gets what.
OneLake's AI governance engine automatically determines access based on Microsoft Entra job titles.
fields.correctAnswer: The data engineer or workspace admin assigns roles (Admin / Member / Contributor / Viewer) — Fabric enforces the roles but does not decide who gets what.
fields.rationale: Role assignment is a human decision — only the team knows who should be Admin vs Viewer. Fabric ENFORCES the four workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) but cannot DECIDE the assignments. The most common Junior confusion is hoping for an AI/auto-detect role assignment; access policy is always a human-in-the-loop step.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Default-allow-all would be a security disaster. Workspaces require explicit role grants.

Option C: Invents a non-existent AI role-assignment engine.

tasks.title: Assign NordGrid Data to Medallion Layers

description.context: The Bronze-Silver-Gold (medallion) architecture is the standard layered design for lakehouses. BRONZE is raw ingested data — same bytes as received from the source system, with at most ingestion metadata (load_ts, source_file) added. No transformation, no schema enforcement. SILVER is cleaned and conformed: schema enforced, types tightened, nulls handled, duplicates removed, and reference data joined for ENRICHMENT (joining substation_id to substation_name is Silver, not Gold). GOLD is business-ready: pre-computed aggregates and denormalized tables shaped for a specific consumer (a dashboard, a report, an ML feature store). The discriminator is not file format or refresh frequency — it is what TRANSFORMATIONS have been applied.
description.task: For each data item, identify which medallion layer it belongs to.
description.validationHint: Bronze = raw, untransformed, as-received. Silver = cleaned, validated, typed, deduplicated. Gold = aggregated, denormalized, business-ready.

fields.label: A CSV file copied from NordGrid's external SFTP server at 06:00 this morning. No columns were removed, no rows were filtered, no types were changed. An ingestion timestamp was added.
options: Bronze — raw data as received, with only ingestion metadata (load_ts) added. No transformation = Bronze.
Silver — the CSV was ingested into Fabric, so it has been processed and qualifies as Silver-stage data.
Gold — CSV is a structured exchange format, which makes the data business-ready and consumer-facing.
fields.correctAnswer: Bronze — raw data as received, with only ingestion metadata (load_ts) added. No transformation = Bronze.
fields.rationale: Bronze is defined by ABSENCE of transformation. Adding a load timestamp does not move the data into Silver — Bronze is allowed to carry ingestion metadata. The most common Junior confusion is treating 'arrived in Fabric' as 'processed'; arrival into the Bronze landing zone is by definition still Bronze.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Confuses ingestion (moving) with transformation (changing). Bronze is the landing layer.

Option C: Confuses file format with business readiness. CSV is a format; Gold is about denormalized aggregates shaped for a consumer.

fields.label: Meter readings with an enforced schema (meter_id as string, daily_kw as double, date as date), with null meter_id rows removed, duplicates on (meter_id, date) deduplicated, and negative daily_kw filtered out. Stored as a partitioned Delta table.
options: Bronze — it is stored as a Delta table; Bronze is wherever data first lands inside Fabric, including Delta-formatted landings.
Silver — schema enforced, types tightened, nulls dropped, duplicates removed, business invariants applied. The textbook Silver shape.
Gold — Delta tables with partitioning are a Gold-layer storage pattern; partitioned Delta = Gold.
fields.correctAnswer: Silver — schema enforced, types tightened, nulls dropped, duplicates removed, business invariants applied. The textbook Silver shape.
fields.rationale: Silver is defined by the cleaning/conforming transformations: schema enforcement, type tightening, deduplication, quality filters. All four are present here, so this is Silver. The most common Junior confusion is mistaking partitioned Delta for a Gold marker — Delta + partitioning is just a storage choice; the LAYER is determined by the transformations performed, not the file format.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Confuses storage format with layer. Bronze can be Delta or files; the layer is about transformation depth.

Option C: Confuses partitioning (a storage optimization) with aggregation (the actual Gold marker).

fields.label: A pre-computed table containing monthly average energy consumption per region, with columns region, month, avg_daily_kw, total_meters, and total_kw. Refreshed weekly for the reporting team's Power BI dashboard.
options: Bronze — refreshed weekly from external Silver sources, so it is a freshly-ingested raw extract.
Silver — the columns are validated and typed, and Silver is the layer that holds typed business data.
Gold — a denormalized, pre-computed aggregate (region x month) shaped for a specific consumer (Power BI dashboard). Aggregation + consumer-shaped = Gold.
fields.correctAnswer: Gold — a denormalized, pre-computed aggregate (region x month) shaped for a specific consumer (Power BI dashboard). Aggregation + consumer-shaped = Gold.
fields.rationale: Gold is defined by AGGREGATION and CONSUMER-SHAPING. This table aggregates per (region, month) and is built specifically for the dashboard — that's Gold. The most common Junior confusion is mistaking refresh frequency or 'pretty columns' for the layer marker; the actual marker is whether the data is BUSINESS-READY for a specific consumer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Refresh frequency does not determine layer. Bronze is about raw ingestion from external systems, not weekly aggregations.

Option B: Silver validates individual records; aggregation is the Gold step.

fields.label: A JSON response from NordGrid's weather API, stored in the Lakehouse Files section exactly as received. Contains nested fields (station_id, temp_c, wind_speed, forecast array) with no schema enforcement.
options: Bronze — raw API response stored as-received in the Files section, no schema enforcement, no transformation. Textbook Bronze.
Silver — JSON is a structured format with named fields, so it qualifies as conformed/typed data and lives in Silver.
Gold — weather data is intended to enrich meter readings for the forecasting team, so its purpose makes it Gold.
fields.correctAnswer: Bronze — raw API response stored as-received in the Files section, no schema enforcement, no transformation. Textbook Bronze.
fields.rationale: Bronze is the layer for raw, as-received payloads. JSON is just a format — without schema enforcement, type tightening, or any transformation, it stays Bronze. The most common Junior confusion is conflating 'JSON has named fields' with 'JSON is structured/Silver'; Silver requires the engineer to ENFORCE a schema, not just to receive one.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Confuses file format with data quality. JSON alone is not Silver; explicit schema enforcement is.

Option C: Confuses intended use (enrichment) with current state (raw).

fields.label: Meter readings joined with substation metadata (substation_name, capacity_mw) and customer reference data (customer_type). Rows with null substation_id after the join were flagged with is_enriched = false rather than dropped.
options: Bronze — null substation_id values mean the data is not fully clean, so it stays in the raw Bronze layer until those nulls are resolved.
Silver — reference-data ENRICHMENT (substations, customer type) with explicit quality flags is a textbook Silver transformation. Same row grain, more columns.
Gold — combining multiple source tables into one is a multi-source aggregation pattern, which is Gold by definition.
fields.correctAnswer: Silver — reference-data ENRICHMENT (substations, customer type) with explicit quality flags is a textbook Silver transformation. Same row grain, more columns.
fields.rationale: Silver covers both cleaning AND ENRICHMENT (joining reference dimensions). The grain is the same (one row per meter reading); we just added context columns. Quality flags (is_enriched) are a Silver pattern — they keep the row but warn downstream. The most common Junior confusion is treating 'multi-table join' as a Gold marker; enrichment joins (preserving grain) belong in Silver, while aggregation joins (collapsing grain) live in Gold.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Quality flags are Silver hygiene, not Bronze rawness.

Option C: Confuses enrichment joins (Silver) with aggregation (Gold).

fields.label: A ranked list of the top 10 highest-consuming meters per region for the current quarter, with columns rank, meter_id, region, quarterly_total_kw, and customer_type. Computed from Silver readings and served to the operations team through a Warehouse view.
options: Bronze — derived from Silver, so it sits 'below' Silver in the medallion stack and counts as Bronze.
Silver — built on quality-validated data with proper types, so it inherits the Silver classification.
Gold — pre-computed business ranking (top 10 per region per quarter), aggregated, served to a specific consumer team. Aggregation + consumer-shaped + materialized view = Gold.
fields.correctAnswer: Gold — pre-computed business ranking (top 10 per region per quarter), aggregated, served to a specific consumer team. Aggregation + consumer-shaped + materialized view = Gold.
fields.rationale: Gold sits ABOVE Silver, not below — Bronze -> Silver -> Gold flows in increasing refinement. A pre-computed ranking that aggregates Silver into a top-10-per-region view for the operations team is Gold. The most common Junior confusion is inverting the stack ('derived from = beneath') or treating quality-clean data as automatically Silver; layer is determined by the transformations APPLIED, and aggregation is the Gold marker.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inverts the medallion stack. Gold is above Silver.

Option B: Confuses data quality (Silver) with business optimization for a consumer (Gold).

description.context: Fabric capacity is the SHARED compute pool that every workload (notebooks, pipelines, dataflows, SQL, Power BI) draws from. It is metered in Capacity Units (CUs) over time — effectively CU-seconds. Total CU consumption for one job is roughly compute_intensity x duration. A 25-minute Spark notebook on 500K rows is 100s-1000s of times more expensive in CU-seconds than an 8-second SQL query, even when the SQL touches the same row count, because compute_intensity and duration both matter. When two workloads share a capacity, exceeding the SKU's CU/sec causes throttling — both jobs slow down. Reducing total CU consumption (faster code, fewer shuffles) is the only way to permanently reduce capacity pressure; moving workspaces in the same capacity does NOT help.
description.task: Given three NordGrid activities with their described resource profiles, predict the relative capacity consumption and identify which activity the team should monitor most closely.
description.validationHint: Capacity consumption depends on both compute intensity and duration. A 45-minute Spark job processing millions of rows consumes far more CU-seconds than a 2-minute dataflow refreshing 200 rows.

fields.label:
Activity A: A PySpark notebook transforms 500,000 meter readings from Bronze to Silver. It reads CSV files, enforces schemas, deduplicates, filters invalid rows, and writes partitioned Delta tables. Runtime: 25 minutes.

Activity B: A Dataflow Gen2 refreshes NordGrid's substation reference table — 200 rows from an external database. It renames two columns and writes to a Lakehouse table. Runtime: 90 seconds.

Activity C: A T-SQL query in the Gold Warehouse computes monthly regional totals from the Silver readings table (500,000 rows, GROUP BY region and month). Runtime: 8 seconds.

Which activity consumes the MOST capacity units?
options: Activity A — Spark notebook, 25 min on 500K rows. Compute_intensity x duration dominates: 25 minutes of Spark CU is orders of magnitude more than 90s of dataflow or 8s of SQL.
Activity B — dataflows use a separate billing engine and dataflow refreshes are billed at premium CU rates, so even a short refresh outweighs longer Spark runs.
Activity C — querying 500K rows in 8 seconds is compute-intensive on a per-second basis, and the Warehouse engine charges higher CU rates than Spark.
All three consume roughly equal capacity — Fabric normalizes CU consumption across workloads to give a flat per-job cost regardless of duration or data volume.
fields.correctAnswer: Activity A — Spark notebook, 25 min on 500K rows. Compute_intensity x duration dominates: 25 minutes of Spark CU is orders of magnitude more than 90s of dataflow or 8s of SQL.
fields.rationale: CU consumption is roughly compute_intensity x duration. Activity A runs 25 minutes on a multi-node Spark cluster — that dwarfs 90s of dataflow on 200 rows and 8s of SQL even on 500K rows. The most common Junior confusion is judging consumption by data volume alone (C touches 500K rows so it must be expensive); duration is the multiplier that makes A dominant.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Dataflows do not have a separate billing system that overrides duration.

Option C: 8 seconds is tiny. Query duration is what matters, not row count alone.

Option D: Fabric meters by actual CU-seconds; jobs are not flat-priced.

fields.label: NordGrid schedules Activity A (Silver notebook) at 06:00 daily. The analytics team runs a large Power BI dashboard refresh at 06:15 on the same capacity. During the overlap, both workloads run slower than usual. Why?
options: Same Fabric capacity = same shared CU/sec budget. When two workloads' combined demand exceeds the SKU's CU/sec ceiling, the platform throttles both. Capacity contention.
Power BI cannot read from Delta tables while a notebook is writing to them; Delta blocks readers during writes, so the dashboard waits.
The Spark notebook acquires an exclusive lock on the entire OneLake storage account, preventing Power BI from reading any tables until it finishes.
This is a Fabric bug — different workloads (Spark + Power BI) are isolated by design and should never affect each other's performance.
fields.correctAnswer: Same Fabric capacity = same shared CU/sec budget. When two workloads' combined demand exceeds the SKU's CU/sec ceiling, the platform throttles both. Capacity contention.
fields.rationale: A Fabric capacity provides a fixed CU/sec budget. When concurrent workloads together exceed it, Fabric throttles work to stay within the budget — both jobs slow down. The most common Junior confusion is thinking different workload types are isolated; in fact ALL workloads on the same capacity share the same CU pool.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Delta supports concurrent reads and writes via its log; readers don't wait for writers.

Option C: Invents a OneLake-wide lock that doesn't exist.

Option D: SaaS shared capacity is by design, not a bug.

fields.label: NordGrid's data engineering lead wants to reduce the capacity impact of the daily Silver notebook. Which approach directly reduces CU consumption?
options: Move the notebook to a different workspace within the same capacity — workspaces have independent CU pools, so moving the notebook offloads the work onto a separate budget.
Optimize the PySpark code (fewer shuffles, predicate pushdown, column pruning) so the notebook finishes in 12 minutes instead of 25. Less duration = less CU x time = less consumption.
Schedule the notebook at midnight instead of 06:00 — off-peak hours give the same job a discounted CU rate, so total consumption drops.
Switch from PySpark to Spark SQL — SQL queries are billed at a lower CU rate than PySpark code, so the same work costs less.
fields.correctAnswer: Optimize the PySpark code (fewer shuffles, predicate pushdown, column pruning) so the notebook finishes in 12 minutes instead of 25. Less duration = less CU x time = less consumption.
fields.rationale: CU consumption equals compute_intensity x duration. The only durable way to reduce it is to do LESS WORK — optimize the code so it finishes faster. Moving workspaces (within the same capacity) doesn't change the CU pool; rescheduling reduces contention but not consumption; the language (PySpark vs Spark SQL) doesn't change billing rates. The most common Junior confusion is hoping for a configuration knob; the only knob is 'make the code do less'.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Workspaces within the same capacity SHARE the CU pool.

Option C: Reschedule reduces contention, not total CU.

Option D: PySpark vs Spark SQL: same engine, same CU rate; what matters is the work performed.

tasks.title: Trace NordGrid's Meter Reading Through Fabric

description.context: Fabric's end-to-end data flow chains a few core artifacts: external sources land into Bronze via Data Factory's Copy activity; Spark notebooks transform Bronze to Silver Delta tables; the Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint auto-generates over Silver tables (read-only); Warehouses persist Gold-layer aggregates; Power BI consumes Gold via Direct Lake (reads OneLake files in place — no copy, no DirectQuery round trip). Critically, Fabric uses OneLake as the single physical store across the journey: Bronze files, Silver Delta, and Gold Warehouse all live in the same OneLake. Components that only READ from OneLake (SQL endpoint, Power BI Direct Lake) do NOT create new physical copies. Counting the actual storage writes in this journey is what tests whether you understand 'one copy of data, many engines'.
description.task: Arrange the 8 stages of the reading's journey in the correct order, from external source to dashboard. Then identify which medallion layer applies at two key stages.
description.validationHint: The journey follows the medallion pattern: raw ingestion (Bronze) → validation and enrichment (Silver) → aggregation (Gold) → visualization. Each stage uses a different Fabric component.

fields.label: What is the FIRST Fabric component that acts on the reading after it leaves the external SFTP server?
options: A Fabric notebook reads the CSV directly from SFTP and transforms it; notebooks own external ingestion in modern Fabric.
A Data Factory pipeline (Copy activity) pulls the CSV from SFTP and lands it in a Bronze Lakehouse. External ingestion is Data Factory's job.
The SQL analytics endpoint queries the SFTP file directly via External Tables, making the reading queryable in T-SQL before any landing.
Power BI ingests the reading directly from SFTP via a Power Query connector and lands it in its semantic model.
fields.correctAnswer: A Data Factory pipeline (Copy activity) pulls the CSV from SFTP and lands it in a Bronze Lakehouse. External ingestion is Data Factory's job.
fields.rationale: Data Factory's Copy activity is Fabric's external-ingestion workhorse — it pulls files from SFTP, S3, on-prem databases, etc., and lands them in OneLake (Bronze). Notebooks transform data already inside Fabric; they don't own the pull from external sources. The most common Junior confusion is reading 'notebook' as the entry point because notebook code is more visible; the pipeline runs first.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Notebooks transform ingested data, not external pulls.

Option C: SQL endpoint reads OneLake tables, not SFTP.

Option D: Power BI doesn't ingest raw external files in production architectures.

fields.label: After the CSV file lands in the Bronze Lakehouse's Files section, what happens next?
options: The SQL analytics endpoint automatically makes the CSV queryable in T-SQL once the file lands in Files; raw CSV is queryable without any additional step.
A Fabric notebook reads the CSV from Bronze Files, validates schema, filters invalid rows, deduplicates, and writes a clean Delta table to Silver. Bronze->Silver = Spark notebook.
Power BI directly imports the raw CSV from Bronze and builds a report; the medallion architecture is optional in modern Fabric.
A Dataflow Gen2 automatically transforms every file that lands in the Files section without any explicit trigger or schedule.
fields.correctAnswer: A Fabric notebook reads the CSV from Bronze Files, validates schema, filters invalid rows, deduplicates, and writes a clean Delta table to Silver. Bronze->Silver = Spark notebook.
fields.rationale: Bronze-to-Silver is the canonical Spark notebook job — schema enforcement, deduplication, and quality filters happen in PySpark, with the result written as Delta. The most common Junior confusion is hoping the SQL endpoint queries raw CSVs in Files; the SQL endpoint only sees Delta tables in the Tables section, not raw files.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: SQL endpoint queries Tables (Delta), not Files (raw).

Option C: Skips Silver/Gold; in production architectures Power BI consumes Gold, not raw.

Option D: Dataflows are explicitly triggered/scheduled, not auto-watching folders.

fields.label: The reading is now a row in the Silver Lakehouse's Delta table. What Fabric artifact automatically makes this row queryable with T-SQL, without any additional configuration?
options: A Data Factory pipeline that exposes the table to SQL users; the engineer must add a 'SQL Expose' activity per Delta table.
The SQL analytics endpoint — Fabric auto-generates one per Lakehouse, read-only T-SQL over every Delta table in the Tables section. Zero config required.
A Fabric Warehouse that the engineer creates manually and synchronizes nightly with the Lakehouse Delta tables.
A Power BI semantic model that translates Delta files into a queryable SQL surface.
fields.correctAnswer: The SQL analytics endpoint — Fabric auto-generates one per Lakehouse, read-only T-SQL over every Delta table in the Tables section. Zero config required.
fields.rationale: Every Lakehouse in Fabric ships with an automatically generated SQL analytics endpoint that exposes its Tables section as READ-ONLY T-SQL. There's no setup; it appears alongside the Lakehouse. The most common Junior confusion is conflating Lakehouse + SQL endpoint with Warehouse — they are different artifacts: SQL endpoint is read-only auto-generated, Warehouse is read-write manually-created.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Pipelines orchestrate; they don't expose tables to SQL.

Option C: Warehouse is a separate manual artifact, not the auto-generated SQL surface.

Option D: Power BI semantic models are for BI consumption, not generic T-SQL access.

fields.label: An analyst writes a T-SQL query in the Gold Warehouse: SELECT region, SUM(daily_kw) FROM silver_readings WHERE month = 3 GROUP BY region. NordGrid's reading for M-0042 (1,847.3 kW, NORTH region) is included in the NORTH region's March total. Where does this aggregated result live?
options: Bronze — derived from raw meter data, so it sits at the bottom of the medallion stack.
Silver — the source table is Silver, so the aggregated output inherits the Silver classification.
Gold — a pre-computed business aggregate (region monthly totals) stored in the Warehouse for reporting consumers. The destination determines the layer.
fields.correctAnswer: Gold — a pre-computed business aggregate (region monthly totals) stored in the Warehouse for reporting consumers. The destination determines the layer.
fields.rationale: The layer is determined by the DESTINATION (where the data is stored and how it is shaped), not by the source. Even though the query reads from Silver, the aggregated result stored in the Gold Warehouse for a consumer team is Gold. The most common Junior confusion is inheriting the source's layer; in reality each materialization is classified by its own shape and consumer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inverts direction — Bronze is raw, not derived.

Option B: Confuses source layer with destination layer; the materialized output's role is what counts.

fields.label: The Power BI dashboard shows the NORTH region's March energy total (which includes M-0042's 1,847.3 kW). How does Power BI access this Gold-layer data in Fabric?
options: Power BI imports a copy of the Gold data into its own VertiPaq storage on a refresh schedule (legacy Import mode); a fresh duplicate exists in the model.
Power BI uses Direct Lake mode — reads OneLake's Parquet files in place, no copy, no DirectQuery round trip. Same physical files as the Warehouse, queried directly.
The data engineer exports a CSV from the Warehouse and uploads it to Power BI; Power BI cannot natively read Fabric tables.
Power BI uses DirectQuery, sending every visual to the Warehouse engine for execution and round-tripping each query at view time.
fields.correctAnswer: Power BI uses Direct Lake mode — reads OneLake's Parquet files in place, no copy, no DirectQuery round trip. Same physical files as the Warehouse, queried directly.
fields.rationale: Direct Lake is Fabric's distinctive Power BI storage mode — Power BI reads OneLake Parquet files directly, no IMPORT (no scheduled copy into VertiPaq) and no DirectQuery (no per-visual round trip to a remote engine). It combines Import speed with DirectQuery freshness. The most common Junior confusion is mixing Direct Lake / DirectQuery / Import — each is a distinct storage mode, and Direct Lake is the one specific to Fabric.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Import mode copies; Direct Lake eliminates that copy.

Option C: A manual anti-pattern; Power BI reads Fabric Lakehouse/Warehouse natively.

Option D: DirectQuery round-trips per visual; Direct Lake reads files directly without a remote engine call.

fields.label: Looking at the complete journey — SFTP → Pipeline → Bronze Lakehouse → Notebook → Silver Lakehouse → SQL endpoint → Gold Warehouse → Power BI — how many times was the underlying data physically copied between storage locations?
options: Seven times — every arrow in the journey is a physical copy, including SQL endpoint reads and Power BI consumption.

Three times — SFTP to Bronze (Copy activity write), Bronze to Silver (notebook write), Silver to Gold (Warehouse aggregate write). The SQL endpoint reads in place; Power BI Direct Lake reads in place.
Once — OneLake stores everything in one location, so data is materialized once and the rest are views over the same bytes.
Zero — Fabric uses shortcuts for the entire journey, so no data movement occurs anywhere in the pipeline.
fields.correctAnswer: Three times — SFTP to Bronze (Copy activity write), Bronze to Silver (notebook write), Silver to Gold (Warehouse aggregate write). The SQL endpoint reads in place; Power BI Direct Lake reads in place.
fields.rationale: Three physical writes: (1) Copy activity lands the SFTP file into Bronze, (2) the notebook writes a new Delta table into Silver, (3) the Warehouse query materializes a new Gold aggregate. The SQL endpoint and Power BI Direct Lake do NOT create copies — they read OneLake files in place. The most common Junior confusion is counting every arrow as a copy (overcounts) or thinking OneLake means zero copies (undercounts) — only the actual write steps move data.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: SQL endpoint and Direct Lake are read-in-place; not every arrow is a copy.

Option C: Layers are different materializations; data IS rewritten Bronze to Silver to Gold.

Option D: Confuses shortcuts (references) with the actual pipeline writes.

conceptsCombined: Data Factory's role as the ingestion orchestrator (Lesson 5, 10)
SaaS-managed artifacts: the auto-generated SQL analytics endpoint (Lesson 3, 10)
Capacity and compute: understanding that OneLake enables in-place reading without copies (Lesson 8)
Data engineer's role in the pipeline: the notebook transformation sits at the center (Lesson 9)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This task traces a single meter reading through the entire Fabric platform, requiring the student to recall which component handles which step, which layer applies at each stage, and how Fabric's unified storage model (OneLake) reduces data copying compared to the platform sprawl scenario from Task 1. It synthesizes the module's core narrative: Fabric exists to unify these components into a single platform where data flows through layers without fragmentation.

The practice set uses 3 concept identification + 3 output prediction tasks with no write-the-code tasks. The normal §4.2 max of 2 per task type is exceeded under §4.3. The synthesis task (F1-task-06) is typed as output_prediction but serves the synthesis role, combining 5 concepts from across the module's 10 lessons. No code synthesis is possible because code is not introduced until Module F5.
selfCheck.theoryPracticeBoundary: The theory traces NordGrid's data flow at a high level in Lesson 10 (The Life of Data in Fabric). The practice synthesis task (Task 6) asks the student to trace the same flow but through specific decision points: which component acts first, what artifact is auto-generated, which layer applies at each stage, and how many physical copies occur. This tests application of the mental model, not recall of the diagram from the lesson. Tasks 1–5 test individual concepts (sprawl, workloads, SaaS, layers, capacity) that the theory introduces separately — the practice requires the student to apply each concept to a new NordGrid scenario not used in the theory.
selfCheck.crossModuleNotes: This practice set tests only Module F1 concepts. No knowledge from Modules F2–F10 is required. The SQL analytics endpoint is mentioned in Task 6 but only at the level taught in F1 Lesson 10 (it exists and auto-generates); the detailed F4 and F9 content is not needed.
